_comment: The Elf voice (NPCConversation II.1b, SpeciesVoice). speech: the rules run over any shared line they say. voice: openers and closers. thought: their own thoughts by situation. script: two-person scripts, speaker 0 is always the Elf.

openers: If you will permit an elder,
As my mother said in the old tongue,
Between the leaves and the stars,
I have watched kingdoms fall, and
With the patience of an oak,
As the old songs have it,
I hear it before you do:
One learns, in a few centuries,
closers: Or so the centuries tell me.
I shall remember it longer than you.
Mark it, in a hundred years.
Forgive my ears for hearing it.
As it was in my youth.
It will pass. Most things do.
With the grace of the old forests.
Some things are worth the wait.

generic: The rosebushes along this street have been pruned by a butcher. I {weep|sigh|despair} a little.
Three centuries of practice and my braid still will not sit right on {Mondays|rainy days|market days}.
That young man will be old by the time I finish this {book|tapestry|sonnet}. Poor thing.
My ears caught a quarrel three streets away. Mortals argue so passionately about so little.
I must restring my {lute|harp|bow} tonight. The damp gets into everything here.
That building was new when I last passed. Now it is charming. Give it a century, it will be beautiful.
Somebody is whistling an air I wrote in {1740|1802|1655}. Badly, but with feeling.
I should water the {orchids|ferns|lemon tree}. They sulk if I am late, and so do I.
Every year the shop windows get brighter and the shopkeepers ruder.
A hawk overhead. Two hundred paces up, and it has a sparrow in mind. I do not envy the sparrow.
I set a sapphire this morning. Perfect. I shall not touch another stone until I calm down.
People keep asking my age. I keep answering {'old enough'|'older than your town'|'rude question'}.
The Guild sent me another letter. Sealed with wax. At least they remember how letters should look.
I bought a television. It is loud and very small and everyone in it is in a hurry.
There is a {wren|robin|thrush} nesting in my window box. I have rearranged my week around it.
Mortal fashion changes so fast. I wore this coat in 1890 and it has come back twice.
The leylines hum a little sour today. Somebody upstream is dampening them, I expect.
I could outwait this queue. I could outwait this whole building, frankly.
The baker's daughter has her grandfather's nose. I remember his grandfather's nose too.
Sunlight through linden leaves. Nobody else has even looked up. Their loss.
My {gloves|boots|cloak} cost more than that car. They will also outlast it.
A child just asked if my ears are real. I asked if her nose was. We are even.
The clocks here all disagree by a minute. As if a minute mattered to anyone.
I have been meaning to learn to drive properly. Since 1923. There is no rush.
The choir at {the church|the school|the station} sang flat again. I said nothing. Heroically.
Another new building of glass and grey. Mortals build mirrors and then hate what they see.
I should write my memoirs. I keep starting, and then another century happens.
One grey hair. One. I shall have it framed, or burned.
The florist has finally learned to wrap peonies properly. It only took her thirty years.
I can hear the radio in the flat below. Every song lasts three minutes. How do they fall in love so fast?
My bow has not been drawn in a year. It is beginning to look at me reproachfully.
The old elm in the square is ill. Nobody notices. I notice.
They put a vending machine where the fountain used to be. Progress, they call it.
Today I shall be patient with everyone. It is a small enchantment, and a hard one.
A pigeon has landed beside me and is judging my posture. I am judging its plumage. Truce.
I wore silver today. Silver is for days when one expects to be admired.
Mortals say 'in my day'. I have had so many days I no longer know which one is mine.
Someone has painted their door a perfect shade of moss green. I may call on them, simply to say so.
The stars over this town are dimmed by streetlamps. I remember them brighter. I remember everything brighter.
My cousin writes that Varlenia is {lovely|dreadful|lovely and dreadful} this season. As always.

sleep: A short rest with my eyes half open, and I shall be myself again.
Even an elf frays without sleep. Mine are fraying at the {edges|ears|temper}.
I need linen sheets and an open window. The night has been talking without me.
Too long awake. My reflection looks almost three hundred.
Sleep, a little. The stars will keep watch. They have done it longer than I have.
Bed. Before I say something unkind about someone's taste in curtains.
hunger: I could eat. Something with herbs in it, please, not something with a wrapper.
A pear, a little cheese, a glass of white wine. Is that so much to ask of a city?
Hungry. It is so undignified. My stomach has no sense of occasion.
The smell from that {bakery|kitchen|market stall} has quite undone my composure.
I forgot to eat again. One gets lost admiring things.
Elves can go a long time without food. A long time is now over.
work: Back to the {workshop|embassy|greenhouse}. Beauty does not make itself, sadly.
A client wants their ring by Friday. Friday! I have spent longer choosing a stone.
My employer is forty and calls me 'young lady'. I let him. It amuses me.
Another day of diplomacy. Smile, nod, remember everything they will forget.
I have done this work for ninety years. I still find new ways to do it better.
Work, then a long evening. Mortals do it the other way round and wonder why they are tired.
leisure: I need an afternoon with a book, a willow and absolutely nobody.
A concert tonight. If the cellist is poor I shall leave quietly and loudly.
My harp has been quiet too long. So have I.
I should go to the {gallery|opera|botanical garden}. My soul is beginning to look shabby.
A long walk among old trees. They are the only ones who never interrupt.
Archery at dawn, poetry at dusk. Anything in between is negotiable.
crime: That {necklace|brooch|ring} is wasted on its owner. No. Elegance does not steal.
I could take it and be gone before they blinked. I have been faster than mortals for centuries.
A theft would be so vulgar. A clever theft, though... no.
Nobody watches an elf's hands. They are always looking at the ears.
I have outlived three police forces in this city. The fourth looks keener.
Patience. If I want it badly enough, its owner will die of old age eventually.
hygiene: I need a bath with rosemary in it. And a comb. And an hour of nobody knocking.
My hair is a disgrace. An elf with tangled hair is a sad omen.
There is city dust on my sleeves. I feel like an old statue.
I smell of {bus|crowd|chip shop}. This cannot continue.
Clean water, lavender soap, a long mirror. The basic dignities.
My ears need cleaning. You have no idea what they collect. Neither do I, and I prefer it so.
money: Only {forty|sixty|ninety} euros until the end of the month. My jewels look at me hopefully.
My family is in Varlenia, drowning in money. I am here, wading in rent.
I could sell a ring. Each one remembers someone, though.
Money comes and goes. I have watched fortunes rise and fall like tides. Mine is low tide.
Poverty is so inelegant. I must be poor beautifully, then.
A commission or two would help. Somebody must want a song about their dog.
safety: Something moves in that alley. My ears say two of them, and not friendly.
I would feel safer with my bow. I would feel safest with my bow and a high window.
This street feels wrong. I have survived four centuries by trusting that feeling.
A long life is a careful life. I shall take the lit road.
The air tastes of a bubble nearby. Time is sour here. Best walk away slowly.
Footsteps behind me, fifty paces. They think I cannot hear them. Mortals.
comfort: A velvet chair, a fire, a good vintage. I have earned them several times over.
My rooms are too small for my furniture, and my furniture is too old for this century.
I miss the garden terrace at my mother's house. Not the house. The terrace.
Silk cushions. Is it vain to want silk cushions? It is. I want them anyway.
A quiet room that faces east. That is all an elf needs. And a harp. And a view.
This bench is very hard and very modern. Two qualities I distrust.
social: I have not had a proper conversation in weeks. Everyone here speaks in headlines.
I miss my friends. Most of them are statues now, or portraits, or both.
A dinner party. Candles, long talk, someone wrong about Byron. I need it.
Mortals make friends so quickly. Teach me. I take about thirty years.
I should call on the {florist|old professor|lady upstairs}. She always has gossip and good tea.
Loneliness lasts longer in an elf. I would rather not let it settle.

rain: Rain on the linden leaves. The city finally sounds like music.
My hair and the rain have an old quarrel. The rain is winning today.
Rain is just the sky remembering something. I know the feeling.
Mortals run from the rain. I walk. My cloak was made for this, in {1801|1777|1840}.
The gardens will be grateful. The gardeners, less so.
Soft rain, the kind that makes moss proud.
storm: Thunder. Somewhere a god is in a mood. Not my concern.
A proper storm. I have not seen one like it since the winter of {1709|1816|1888}.
Lightning is the only light that hurries and still looks beautiful.
My ears ache with the pressure. Elves feel a storm a day before it comes.
The old oak will hold. The new fence will not. Lesson in that.
I shall watch it from the window with a glass of something red. Storms deserve an audience.
snow: Snow. Every flake different, and they melt before anyone looks. How mortal of them.
The city is silent under snow. At last, a city with manners.
I left no footprints. Old habit. The children were very cross.
Snow on pine branches. I could look at it for a decade.
Mortals curse the snow and then build little people out of it. Endearing.
The cold makes my ears go pink. It is the one flaw I allow myself.
clear: Clear skies. I can see the hills forty miles off, and a crow on each of them.
A blue day. The kind of day mortals waste indoors.
Sunlight on old stone. My favourite colour has no name in your language.
Not a cloud. The sky is showing off, and I approve.
Fine weather for archery. Or for sitting in a garden pretending to read.
Such clear air. The {cathedral|river|old castle} looks almost as fine as it did when it was new.

morning: Dawn. The only hour when the whole world is as quiet as an elf.
Morning dew on the roses. I counted the drops once. It took a summer.
Up before the larks, as is proper. The mortals stumble out at eight, grumbling.
A fresh morning. Another day to be patient with everyone. Let us see how long it lasts.
I brushed my hair by the window and watched the {baker|milkman|postman} make his rounds.
The morning light is thin and silver. My favourite metal, my favourite hour.
afternoon: Afternoon. The hour for tea, a book and mild disdain.
The light goes amber about now. Everything looks a century older. It suits the town.
Mortals grow sleepy after lunch. I grow philosophical. It looks the same from outside.
A long afternoon. To me, they are all long. That is rather the point of being me.
Shadows stretching. The trees are pointing at something. They always know.
Halfway through the day and nobody has said anything beautiful. There is still time.
evening: Evening. Candles, wine, and someone to disagree with about music.
The sunset was adequate tonight. Seven out of ten. I am a strict judge.
The first star. I said hello to it. It has been there longer than me, and that is rare.
Evenings were made for singing. Mortals use them for television. Each to their own.
Dusk turns the river to pewter. I shall walk along it slowly, as is proper.
The streetlamps come on one by one, like a shy choir.
night: Night. I see well enough in it. Mortals carry little lights and still trip over things.
The owls are out. They talk such nonsense, but in such lovely voices.
Midnight, and the stars have shifted again. Since the Squishing they do not stay where I left them.
I do not need much sleep. I need much night. There is a difference.
Moonlight on the rooftops. Silver everywhere and nobody awake to steal it.
The city sleeps. I can hear every clock in it, ticking out mortal lives.

SPRING: Spring again. My four hundredth, give or take. It still makes me giddy.
Blossom on the {cherry|almond|apple} trees. Gone in a week. Mortals understand that better than I do.
The sap is rising. I can almost hear it if I put my ear to the bark.
Spring cleaning. I shall air out the tapestries and argue with the moths.
New leaves, young and foolish. I adore them.
SUMMER: Summer. Long evenings, finally the right length for a conversation.
Too hot for velvet. I shall suffer in linen, elegantly.
The roses are at their best. So am I. We are rivals for the season.
A midsummer festival tonight. I know songs for it that nobody else remembers.
Lime trees in flower. The whole street smells like an old love letter.
AUTUMN: Autumn. The most elven of seasons: beautiful, slow, a little proud of its own decline.
The beeches have turned copper. I shall make earrings of the colour, if not the leaves.
Harvest time. Mortals sing more in autumn. I have always noticed.
Fallen leaves on the path. I walk around them. They have had a hard enough day.
A good vintage this year, I can smell it from the vines. I shall open it in fifty years.
WINTER: Winter. The trees sleep and I keep them company with long thoughts.
Bare branches against a white sky. Mortal painters never get the grey right.
Fur collar, silver brooch, and a fire. Winter is simply an excuse to dress well.
Another winter. They come round so quickly, like a song on a jukebox.
Frost on the window in fern shapes. Nature still remembers how to be ornamental.

poor: Darned cuffs and a borrowed bow. I have been rich before. I shall be again, eventually.
My family in Varlenia would not recognise me in this coat. That may be its best feature.
Poor, but my posture is still worth a fortune.
I sold my last good ring for rent. It was a gift from a duchess. She would have understood.
Bread and water, but served on my grandmother's silver plate. One keeps standards.
A long life has its lean decades. This is one. I shall sing through it.
comfortable: Enough to live gracefully, not enough to be vulgar. The ideal balance.
A good flat, a good harp, a good wine on Sundays. I need nothing from Varlenia.
My savings have grown since {1820|1868|1904}. Compound interest is mortal patience, borrowed.
I could afford the opera every week. I go every month, to keep it special.
Comfortable. A word mortals use apologetically. I use it with relish.
A small garden of my own and nobody to tell me how to prune it. Wealth enough.
rich: I have more jewels than days in a year. I wear them in rotation, of course.
My Varlenia estate has a wall, a moat and a leyline damper. Overkill, says my sister. She has two.
Money is easy when one has had four centuries of interest.
I bought the whole orchard so nobody could cut it down. Then I bought the next one.
The bags that fall from the sky over my estate are someone else's problem. I pay people to make sure.
Riches are dull, honestly. But they do keep the rain off a very good hat.

familiar: Those travellers again. Still in a hurry. Still alive. Both are achievements.
I remember that party. One of them has had a haircut. Not a good one.
The road-folk are back. I shall bow, slightly. Slightly is a great honour.
Ah, them. They have aged a little since last time. Mortals do that between visits.
Those travellers walk like people who have seen strange things. I approve of strange things.
They remembered my name. Most mortals remember only the ears.
Back again? Good. I have kept a {song|story|bottle} for them.
That party smells of petrol and adventure. Mostly petrol.
I hope they stay a while. Their kind is so brief, and so interesting.
The camper people again. I heard their engine from the edge of town.
hordeGround: Horde ground. The goblins sing all night. Off-key, but with conviction.
They painted the old fountain black. Corpse paint on marble. I may never recover.
The Horde does not know what to make of an elf. Neither do I, some days.
A goblin asked if my ears were a hat. I said yes. He wants one now.
Under the Horde the gardens have gone wild. Honestly, an improvement on the council's work.
I keep my head down and my bow unstrung. Patience outlasts invasions. I have seen several.
The Horde's banners are hideous. I have offered to redesign them. They took it as a threat.
Junehem on every speaker, every hour. I miss the harpsichord.
A goblin child brought me a {beetle|shiny stone|bottle cap}. A gift. I am oddly moved.
The Horde came from the north, like winter. Winters end. I shall wait.
abroad: The mainland is loud and crowded and alive. Varlenia is quiet and gated and something else.
My mother writes every month asking when I shall come home. I write back about the weather.
Here people ask about my ears. In Varlenia they ask about my charter. I prefer the ears.
I chose a small flat in an old city over an estate in the City of Ghosts. My family thinks I am unwell.
The mortals here have been kind. Rough at the edges, but kind all the way through.
I have a library card, a bicycle and a neighbour who brings soup. I am rich in the wrong ways.
Varlenia has perfect weather. Here it rains on me personally. I find I like that better.
The boat to Varlenia costs a fortune and leaves once a week. I have missed it on purpose for a year.
Old Europe still has trees older than I am. That is why I stay.
My neighbours call me 'the tall one with the ears'. It is the warmest title I have held.

longevity: I watched them light the first gas lamps on this street. Now they are electric. Next, who knows.
Ninety thousand sunsets, and I still stop for a good one.
People ask the secret of a long life. Patience, beauty and never driving over eighty.
I outlived my first love, my second, and my fourth. The third is still writing to me. From Lisbon.
A mortal friend just turned eighty. I bought her flowers I first saw bloom in her grandmother's garden.
The hard part of a long life is not the years. It is the goodbyes.
My passport says born in {1612|1588|1640}. The clerk read it, looked at me, and went for a coffee.
Mortals measure life in years. We measure it in oaks. I am about two oaks old.
varlenia: Varlenia appeared in January and was sold out by March. My uncle was first off the boat.
The City of Ghosts is very beautiful and very pale. The ghosts, I am told, are purely aesthetic.
Body bags fall from the sky in Varlenia. My cousin calls it 'overflow' and changes the subject.
A Varlenian charter costs more than a mortal earns in a lifetime. Several of my lifetimes, honestly.
The gardens in Varlenia are perfect. Too perfect. Nothing grows there that was not paid for.
They dampen the leylines over Varlenia so the magic stays calm. Somewhere else pays for that calm.
Half the elves I know moved to Varlenia. The other half sing sad songs about the first half.
Is Varlenia from another dimension, or the gods' locked room? Nobody there asks, while rents rise.
beauty: Beauty is not vanity. Vanity is not caring when beauty is gone. I care enormously.
A well-cut stone holds light the way a good song holds silence.
Every century has one perfect building. This one is still undecided.
I set emeralds for an empress once. Her neck was shorter than the necklace. We adjusted the empire.
Mortal art is rushed, and that is its genius. You paint as if the light might leave. It might.
Silver tarnishes, gold endures, but silver is the more honest metal.
The ugliest thing in this city is the new car park. The second ugliest is its sign.
An elf without a mirror is like a {harp|bow|garden} without tending. It goes wild.
forests: The old forests remember the elves. The new ones only remember the loggers.
I grow rare orchids in a greenhouse no bigger than a wardrobe. Botany is patience with a watering can.
Some trees speak if you lean close and wait a season. Mostly about the weather.
I planted a yew in {1702|1745|1690}. It is still a teenager.
A forest is a cathedral nobody had to pay for. Do not tell Varlenia.
Every hedgerow is a library. Mortals walk past it reading the road signs.
Mushrooms after rain. I know which ones heal, which ones kill and which ones sing. Do not ask.
Nobody plants an oak for themselves. Except elves. We get to sit in the shade.
archery: A bow is a promise between a tree and a string. The arrow is just the answer.
I can split a hazel wand at a hundred paces. The fairground stall still says I cheat.
Guns are loud, ugly and quick. Like so much of your century.
My bow is older than this country's constitution. Better made, too.
Draw, breathe, release. The same three words for everything worth doing.
The fletching is goose, the shaft is ash, the patience is mine.
A good archer sees the wind. A great one waits for it to change its mind.
I taught a mortal girl to shoot. Ten years later she beat me. I have never been prouder, or crosser.
mortals: Mortals live as if the house were on fire. With the Squishing, perhaps it is.
Your species made the radio, the train and the waffle iron in two centuries. I made a tapestry.
The Guild's pillars stopped ageing by holding a chair. Mortals will do anything to be us.
I envy mortals one thing: you are never bored. You do not have time.
Short lives, loud hearts. Sometimes I think you have the better bargain.
Mortals kept inventing faster ways to travel. Then the Rule of 80 humbled them. I laughed, quietly.
Teach a mortal a song and in three generations it becomes folk music. Flattering, in a way.
They call us condescending. We are simply looking down from a slightly higher century.

positive: {b}, your roses are finally standing up straight. I did nothing. Well. A little.
I wondered why they looked so smug this morning.
They take after their gardener now. Both are improving.
I brought you a pear from the old orchard, {b}. The tree is older than your street.
That's lovely of you, {a}. Thank you.
Eat it slowly. It took two hundred years to get the recipe right.
You sang at the festival last night, {b}. Beautifully. I do not say that often.
Coming from you? I'll take it to my grave.
Please do not hurry there. I would miss the singing.
I fixed the clasp on your necklace while you were out, {b}.
You did? It's been broken for years!
Three years and four months. I counted, and suffered.
Well, thank you. Really.
{b}, would you walk with me along the river? The light is perfect for exactly ten minutes.
Ten minutes? I'm coming, then.
Good. I hate to waste good light on my own.
You remembered my name day, {b}. Nobody has in eighty years.
It was on the calendar in your kitchen.
Then you read my calendar. Even better. Thank you.
Your daughter has a fine eye for stones, {b}. I would take her as an apprentice.
Really? She'd be over the moon.
Tell her it is a long apprenticeship. About forty years.
I'll let her find that out herself.
I wrote a short song about your bakery, {b}. Shall I sing it?
Go on, then.
*sings two lines about warm bread, perfectly in tune*
That's going on a sign above the door.
negative: {b}, you cut down the old lilac. It was older than your mother.
It was the light. You simply did not know how to look at it.
Your radio, {b}. At two in the morning. My ears are not decorative.
Sorry, I fell asleep with it on.
Then I shall sing you awake at five. We shall see who sleeps.
You called me 'grandma' in front of the whole market, {b}.
You told me yourself you're three hundred!
Age is a fact. 'Grandma' is an opinion. Keep your opinions.
This ring you sold me is glass, {b}.
I bought it as real, I swear.
Then we were both cheated. Only one of us should have noticed.
Look, I'll give you your money back.
Must you park that car on my flowerbed, {b}?
And they are public flowers. Far older than your licence.
I sneezed! I sneezed, I promise.
In the second movement. During the rest. I shall remember it for a century.
neutral: Excuse me. Is this the bus to the botanical garden?
Number nine. This is the twelve.
Then I shall admire the twelve until the nine arrives.
Forgive me, do you know a good jeweller in this town?
There's one on the square. Bit pricey.
Pricey is fine. It is 'bad' I cannot tolerate.
What a lovely shade of blue your door is.
Oh. Thanks. My husband picked it.
Then your husband has an eye. Tell him an elf said so.
Is the old chapel on the hill still standing?
The ruin? Mostly. Kids go up there to smoke.
I lit a candle in it once. In 1734. It seems the candle is out.
Pardon me, but your coat is buttoned wrong.
Is it? Oh. So it is.
Now you are elegant. That is all, carry on.
How much are the peonies?
Three euros a stem.
Then I shall have seven, and you will wrap them as if they mattered.
Of course.
Is it always this loud on this street?
Only on market days. And weekends. And most evenings.
So, always. Thank you for your honesty.
Do you know what time the library closes?
Six, I think.
Six. That leaves me two hours, or one good chapter.
I am looking for a quiet café. Somewhere without a television.
Try the one by the bridge. The owner hates TV.
A kindred spirit. Thank you.
Does the river flood here in spring?
Every few years, yeah.
It used to every year. The river is getting lazy. Or wise.
You are staring at my ears.
Sorry! I've never seen an elf up close.
They are real. You may stop looking now, or start paying admission.
Pardon, which way is the old town?
Straight on, then left at the church.
The church with the crooked spire? It was crooked in my youth as well. Thank you.

lines: Your century builds too fast. Nothing here is meant to last.
We don't have centuries, {a}. We build for us.
And your grandchildren inherit car parks.
Better than inheriting nothing at all.
Varlenia is beautiful, but it is beautiful the way a locked jewel case is.
That's what I've always thought about the place.
One should be able to touch beauty. Even if it is only a mortal touch.
Television has ruined conversation, {b}.
Television IS conversation now. Everyone talks about the same shows.
They talk about the same thing. That is not conversation, that is an echo.
Says someone who's been repeating the same opinions since 1800.
The old elm in the square should be protected, not cut down for parking.
Agreed. My grandfather proposed to my grandmother under it.
I was there. She said yes before he finished.
Magic should be learned slowly. Fifty years at least before a first spell.
Fifty years? Most of us would be dead before the exam, {a}.
Then perhaps most of you should not cast spells.
That's easy to say when you've got all the time in the world.
Nothing beats a hand-made thing. Machines make copies. Hands make objects.
My father was a carpenter. He'd have hugged you for that.
Then I shall take the hug as given, and gratefully.

ambient: The light is lovely this evening, {b}.
Thanks, it's been a good year.
Good morning, {b}. You look well rested, for once.
That busker is out of tune, {b}.
The limes are flowering. Smell that.
Can't see a thing without my glasses.
Evening, {b}. Don't let me keep you.
The roses on your wall need cutting back.
Another rainy day. The moss is delighted.
Your cat sat on my harp again, {b}.
Have you seen how tall the poplars have grown?
Too quiet, if you ask me.
The river is high this week, {b}.
